prompt.context: Your client is a multinational pharmaceutical and biologics company. The client has a portfolio of drugs for major disease areas, including cancer, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal diseases, to name a few. The client has experienced a decline in revenue over the last 18 months, and is fearful of further declines, especially given that its most commercially successful drug, which treats acid reflux disease, will be going off of patent in May of next year.
prompt.question: What are the areas they should look into to change the course of this trend?

clarifying_info.q: Can you share revenue data by product or disease area?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — Exhibit 1 shows revenues by disease area.

exhibits.title: Company Revenues by Disease Area (in $B)
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down revenues by drug and disease area, showing each drug's share of 2013 revenues, year-over-year revenue change, and market share trend.

framework: Identify this as a revenue problem — not a cost problem — given the prompt language
Segment revenues: by product/drug, by disease area, by geography (global company)
Assess each product's revenue trajectory and market share position
Investigate patent expiration impact: Purple Pill (acid reflux) goes off-patent next year, opening door to generics
Examine industry/competitive trends: generic entry, regulatory changes, pricing pressure
Evaluate strategic options to defend or replace declining revenue streams

questions.prompt: What are the largest drivers of revenue decline over the last 18 months?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read Exhibit 1 and identify: overall business declining ~10%; Green Pill (Neuroscience) is the largest percentage decline at -40%; Red Pill (Cardiovascular) also declining at -8%. Respiratory (Blue Pill) is the only growth driver at +10%. Candidate should also note the pending Purple Pill patent cliff.

math.setup: Total 2013 revenue = $21B. Calculate 2012 revenue for each drug using the % change, then compute dollar loss.
math.answer: Green Pill is the single largest dollar driver of decline at ~$1B loss year-over-year, followed by Red Pill at ~$400M loss.

questions.prompt: What are some issues that could have caused the Green Pill decline?
questions.guidance: Strong answers include: lower price due to generic competition, lower volume as patients switch to generics, regulatory restrictions, out-of-stocks, currency and geographic trends. The best candidates connect generic entry to declining market share visible in Exhibit 1. Interviewer confirms: ~50% of the Green Pill decline is attributable to generics entering the US and other established markets; remaining declines relate to Medicaid liability and inventory issues.

questions.prompt: Given the Green Pill issues, evaluate the following three options to maintain Purple Pill revenue when it goes off patent next year: (1) Do nothing, (2) License the brand to an OTC manufacturer for $250M one-time fee, (3) Direct-to-patient campaign online with 3rd-party delivery. What would you recommend and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate must work through the math for each option, compare gross profit, and think through short-term vs. long-term dynamics. Key insight: licensing looks close to breakeven in year 1 but generates no recurring revenue in year 2+. Direct-to-patient is the best option if cannibalization stays low. Candidate should surface assumptions about cannibalization risk and incremental volume retention.

math.setup: Assumptions: Total Purple Pill revenue = $3.2B; current margin = 80%; without action, 20% of annual volume is lost to generics (based on Green Pill precedent); over 2/3 of Purple Pill revenue is from the US.
steps: Do nothing: $3.2B x 80% retained = $2.56B revenue x 80% margin = $2.048B gross profit. (Simplified in casebook as $2.5B revenue x 80% = $2.0B gross profit)

License OTC for $250M: Gross profit from retained volume = $2.0B (same as do-nothing base); add $250M one-time fee; subtract cannibalization of 10% of existing volume at 80% margin: 10% x $3.2B x 80% = $256M. Net = $2.0B + $250M - $256M = ~$1.994B gross profit in year 1. No additional $250M in year 2+.
Direct-to-patient: Base retained GP = $2.0B; recover 25% of the 20% lost volume at 50% margin: 20% x 25% x $3.2B x 50% = $0.08B. Total = $2.0B + $0.08B = $2.08B gross profit.
math.answer: Direct-to-patient yields the highest gross profit (~$2.08B) in year 1 and is recurring. Licensing (~$1.994B) is marginally worse than do-nothing (~$2.0B) in year 1 and worse in all subsequent years. Do nothing is better than licensing over a multi-year horizon.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some issues that could have caused the Green Pill revenue decline?

categories.name: Competitive / Generic Entry
ideas: Generic drugs entering the US and other established markets after patent expiry
Loss of market share to lower-priced generics
Price erosion as generics drive down average selling prices

categories.name: Volume Drivers
ideas: Lower tablet sales volume as patients switch to generics
Physician prescribing patterns shifting toward generics
Out-of-stock or supply chain issues reducing available volume

categories.name: Regulatory & Policy
ideas: Formulary changes by payers excluding the branded product

categories.name: Geographic & Macro
ideas: Currency headwinds reducing reported revenues for international markets

recommendation: Pursue the direct-to-patient program (Option 3): it retains the highest gross profit (~$2.08B) and creates a recurring revenue stream, unlike the one-time $250M license fee

Avoid the OTC licensing option: the $250M one-time fee is more than offset by the 10% cannibalization of existing high-margin business, resulting in slightly worse economics than doing nothing — and it contributes nothing in year 2+
If direct-to-patient risks significant cannibalization of the existing 80%-margin hospital/retail channel, model the breakeven carefully and consider pricing adjustments
risks: Direct-to-patient margin is 50% vs. 80% on existing channel — any cannibalization above the assumed 25% retention rate erodes the advantage
Generic penetration could exceed the 20% volume loss assumption, making all options worse than modeled
Licensing deal with OTC partner could damage brand equity if product quality or positioning diverges
next_steps: Quantify cannibalization risk for the direct-to-patient channel with more granular patient data
Model multi-year scenarios (year 2 and beyond) for each option
Explore possibility of a merger, acquisition, or co-promotion deal with another drug producer to backfill declining revenue
Analyze geographic mix: since >2/3 of Purple Pill revenue is US-based, assess US generic timeline and international patent status separately
